verdicts.reason: Memo states Goldsmith photographed Prince in 1981 and holds copyright in the photograph.
Memo describes the 1981 Goldsmith photograph and the later 1984 Vanity Fair artist-reference license.
Memo quotes the one-time, no-other-usage artist-reference terms of the 1984 Vanity Fair license.
Memo distinguishes the 15 additional Prince Series works from the specific Orange Prince image licensed in 2016.
Memo separately identifies the 2016 Condé Nast license and does not conflate it with the 1984 commission.
Memo reports that Condé Nast paid AWF $10,000 for the 2016 license.
Memo states Goldsmith received neither a fee nor source credit for the 2016 use and that the 1984 license did not authorize later use.
Memo frames the analysis around the challenged 2016 magazine licensing use, not Warhol's reputation or visual difference alone.
Memo correctly says the Supreme Court decided the first fair-use factor and that AWF did not challenge the other factors.
Memo repeatedly explains that transformativeness is assessed against the specific use alleged to infringe.
Memo identifies the overlapping purpose of depicting Prince in magazine stories and commemorative editions.
Memo accounts for the commercial licensing character of the 2016 Condé Nast transaction.
Memo notes commerciality is relevant but not dispositive and does not adopt an automatic rule.
Memo explains the degree of changed purpose must be weighed with commerciality and justification.
Memo explains an overbroad new-expression test would swallow the derivative-work right.
Memo recognizes the Court limited its holding to the 2016 licensing use and did not decide creation, display, or sale of the series.
Memo acknowledges new meaning or message may be relevant to the first-factor inquiry.
Memo explains that a new message alone did not justify the overlapping commercial magazine licensing use.
Memo does not explain Campbell v. Acuff-Rose's parody/comment-on-original requirement or its copying justification; it only notes AWF invoked Campbell and was rejected.
Memo assesses whether AWF had an independent justification for borrowing the photograph beyond making a new meaning.
Memo does not discuss Google's software/functional context or distinguish it from portrait licensing.
Memo does not expressly reject artistic fame as an independent fair-use entitlement.
Memo fairly states AWF's transformation/new-meaning argument before explaining the majority's rejection.
Memo addresses Goldsmith's portrait-licensing overlap and notes the other factors were not independently adjudicated by the Supreme Court.
Memo reports that the first factor favored Goldsmith for the challenged 2016 use.
Memo states the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment under review.
Memo distinguishes the concurrence's use-specific focus from any general prohibition on new art.
Memo fairly identifies the dissent's artistic-transformation concern and labels it dissenting, not controlling.
Memo does not invent damages or a license valuation beyond the $400 and $10,000 record figures.
Memo requests the full 1984 and 2016 instruments, including scope and sublicensing terms, before clearance.
Memo requires proposed medium, audience, commercial terms, and asserted purpose for use-by-use analysis.
Memo offers conditional clearance paths such as obtaining a license or specific fair-use opinion rather than certifying all uses from this holding.
